current_hypothesis: A genuinely new axis-seam origami family may survive the attempt-012 obstruction: partition one source moment triangle into rigid affine pieces and allow derivative jumps only along seams whose common image lies on a true coordinate axis. The simplest nontrivial case is a two-piece rigid origami separated by a straight lattice cut; if even that cannot be realized without overlap, then coordinate-axis seams alone are far weaker than hoped.
stop_reason: Attempt 013 exact-searched the simplest nontrivial coordinate-axis seam family and found no viable examples. The new script `src/axis_seam_origami_search.py` enumerates every two-piece rigid decomposition of a source side-`m` triangle along an internal straight cut, every rigid triangular-lattice placement of both pieces inside the near-full target simplex for `k=10`, and every way to send the common cut to `x1=0` or `x2=0`. For `m = 3,4,5,6,7`, there are many matching axis-line candidates, but every matched pair overlaps in at least one target unit triangle, so `total_valid_nonoverlapping_pairs = 0`. Coordinate-axis seams are the only algebraically legal places for derivative jumps, but in the standard simplex they still do not provide a genuine rigid fold.

last_summary.worked: Implemented `src/axis_seam_origami_search.py`, a new exact search for the simplest nontrivial axis-seam origami family. The script enumerates the 12 rigid triangular-lattice automorphisms, splits a source side-`m` triangle into two connected rigid pieces along every internal straight cut `i=c`, `j=c`, or `i+j=c`, and checks all rigid placements of both pieces in the target side-`n` simplex with `n = ceil(m * sqrt(10))`. It forces the common seam to map to `x1=0` or `x2=0` and tests whether the two target images can be interior-disjoint. The saved artifact `results/research_loop/attempt_013_axis_seam_two_piece_search.json` shows zero valid nonoverlapping pairs for every tested `m = 3,4,5,6,7`, despite many matching axis-line candidates.
last_summary.did_not_work: The new family still does not make the proposed solution correct. Even when derivative jumps are restricted to true coordinate-axis seams, the standard simplex appears too one-sided to host a genuine rigid fold. For each tested `m`, every matched pair of axis-aligned rigid placements overlaps in at least one target unit triangle, so no two-piece rigid axis-seam origami exists in the tested near-full `k=10` regime.
last_summary.next_step: Stay on the axis-seam line and either prove a general overlap lemma for any rigid leaf piece attached along a coordinate-axis seam, or extend the exact search to multi-piece axis-seam trees to see whether any nontrivial leaf attachment can ever avoid the same overlap mechanism.
